precepts.text: They mocked the messengers of God, despised his words and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord arose, till there was no remedy.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Elijah cries that the children of Israel have “thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left”. They made a covenant with death and hell. The prophets taught against the rulers and their falsehoods, so the rulers killed the prophets. Chronicles shows how it went all the way to the end of the kingdom.

“But they mocked the messengers of God”: that is what they do now. Look at how they mock the purple and gold, calling us purple Power Rangers. It is the same thing; they mocked us. “and despised his words”: despised his law, like they do now. “and misused his prophets”: had them locked up, exiled, or killed in terrible ways.

“until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.” They pissed the Lord off until there was no remedy left. The killing of the prophets Elijah complained of was not one king’s sin; it was the way of the nation until the wrath came.

precepts.text: Wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people. Those elders brought Babylonian ideas home, the root of the Talmud and the traditions Christ condemned.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Who were the rulers who killed the prophets? The history of Susanna shows where their wickedness came from. “There dwelt a man in Babylon, called Joacim”, a great rich man with a fair garden, “and to him resorted the Jews; because he was more honourable than all others.” He was an elder, a leader, and the people came to sit with him.

“The same year were appointed two of the ancients of the people to be judges, such as the Lord spake of, that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people.” We had ancient judges in Babylon, and they brought Babylonian doctrine and ideals along with them. They seemed to govern the people, but they were not true governors; they were evil and wicked as hell.

These same elders who came out of Babylon, and whose line made its way down to the time of Roman rule, started the Talmud. The Babylonian Talmud: they got it from Babylon. So when Christ condemned their traditions, those traditions came from Babylon. These are the fathers of the Pharisees, the same spirit of the rulers who slew the prophets.

precepts.text: Ahab and Zedekiah prophesied lies in my name and committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and the king of Babylon roasted them in the fire.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Susanna says wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, “such as the Lord spake of”. Where did the Lord speak of it? In Jeremiah, to “all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon”.

“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes”. And the captivity would curse by their names: “The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. He cooked them to death.

Why? “Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them”. That is what your pastors be doing. “even I know, and am a witness, saith the Lord.”

These were the wicked leaders among the people, false prophets instead of the true ones they persecuted. The Pharisees did the exact same thing when Rome ruled: ancient evil from Babylon, from the elders.

precepts.text: I sent my servants the prophets, whom ye have slain and torn in pieces. Your houses will I give to a people that shall come, which not having heard of me yet shall believe me: that is us today.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
The Lord says it through Ezra: “I sent unto you my servants the prophets, whom ye have taken and slain, and torn their bodies in pieces, whose blood I will require of your hands, saith the Lord.” We were doing it to each other. We were killing the prophets of our own people, and he will require that blood.

“Thus saith the Almighty Lord, Your house is desolate, I will cast you out as the wind doth stubble. And your children shall not be fruitful; for they have despised my commandment, and done the thing that is an evil before me.”

“Your houses will I give to a people that shall come; which not having heard of me yet shall believe me; to whom I have shewed no signs, yet they shall do that I have commanded them.” That is us today. We are born again.

Christ said the same in the parable of the vineyard: the husbandmen beat one servant, killed another and stoned another, and last of all killed the son, and the lord of the vineyard “will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen”. The other husbandmen are us today, the people Ezra spoke of. “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.”

precepts.text: O Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, how often would I have gathered thy children together as a hen, and ye would not. Your house is left unto you desolate.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Christ says it to the city: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee”. Over and over again, the same thing Elijah cried about: they slew the prophets.

“how often would I have gathered thy children together”: gathered both kingdoms together, “even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” They refused him, the stone which the builders refused.

“Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.” These are the same words the Lord spoke through Ezra, “Your house is desolate”. The rulers who killed the prophets would kill the Son too, and their house would be left empty, cast out as the wind doth stubble.

precepts.text: Stephen told the council, As your fathers did, so do ye; which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? They were cut to the heart because they knew exactly which grandfathers killed which prophets.
precepts.point: They have thrown down thine altars and slain thy prophets, and I, even I only, am left. Israel's rulers killed the prophets who taught against them. The same people mock the purple and gold today.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Stephen prophesied against the rulers, the builders of his time: “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.” As your fathers did, so do you.

“Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One”. The prophets were killed in the Old Testament, and who were they prophesying of? The Just One. So when the prophets prophesied of a Messiah, they were killed. The killers who got away with it had children, and their children knew who they had killed. Then when Christ was born, they killed him too: “of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers: Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it.”

“When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.” Why cut to the heart? Because they knew. Stephen was in the spirit; he saw their fathers killing the prophets: your father killed Zechariah, your father killed Isaiah. They knew and did not care, and they were pissed off that he said it. They gnashed on him, cursing him out.

The prophets were sent to bring us back to God, and the rulers hated them because the prophets could see right through them. It was the same spirit in Elijah’s day, in Christ’s day, and in Rome against the apostles, and it is the same spirit today.

precepts.text: The Most High told Elijah to anoint Jehu to be king over Israel and Elisha the son of Shaphat to be prophet in his room.
precepts.point: The same pattern continues through the prophets: Elisha was taken from the plow and Amos from the herd.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
The same pattern continues through the prophets. The Most High told Elijah, “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel–meholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.”

As with Samuel at Jesse’s house, the prophet was sent to anoint the one the Most High named.

precepts.text: Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah cast his mantle upon him; he left the care of the literal flock, ministered to Elijah, and eventually became the prophet in his place.
precepts.point: The same pattern continues through the prophets: Elisha was taken from the plow and Amos from the herd.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Elijah “found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” Elisha was taken from the plow.

“And he left the oxen, and ran after Elijah”. He slew a yoke of oxen, “and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave unto the people, and they did eat. Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” He left the care of the literal flock, ministered to Elijah, and eventually became the prophet in his place.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

points: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done and how he had slain all the prophets with the sword. This shows the devil on Ahab: he ran back running his mouth about the slain false prophets and never once mentioned that Elijah had brought rain after a three-year drought.

Jezebel sent a messenger swearing that she would make Elijah's life as the life of one of the slain prophets by the next day. She wanted him dead because he had taken away her power and the name she had gotten in Israel through her idolatry. This is the same wicked spirit named in Revelation, the top-notch wicked woman who feared no God at all.
When Elijah saw it, he arose and went for his life and left his servant behind. He was an old man, not young like Elisha, and he knew Jezebel would truly try to kill him, so he fled.

Elijah went a day's journey into the wilderness, sat down under a juniper tree, and requested that he might die, saying, It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am not better than my fathers.

Our forefathers had ultimate faith and understood regeneration: they could ask the Most High to take their life and let them rest in the grave, trusting he would bring them back whenever he chose. They did not have the lust of the eyes and of this world as their main thought. Elijah counted himself no better than his fathers even though he was great; Christ later called John the Baptist, who came in the spirit of Elijah, the greatest of the prophets.

As Elijah slept, an angel touched him and said, Arise and eat, and there was a cake baking on the coals and a cruise of water at his head. He ate and lay down again; a second time the angel touched him and said the journey was too great for him. He arose and ate, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb, the mount of God. The Most High made food through the angel that sustained Elijah for forty days; that was good spiritual food.

Elijah came to a cave in Horeb and lodged there, and the word of the Lord asked, What doest thou here, Elijah? He answered that he had been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, for the children of Israel had forsaken the covenant, thrown down the altars, and slain the prophets, and he only was left and they sought his life.

The Lord told him to stand upon the mount, and the Lord passed by: a great and strong wind rent the mountains, but the Lord was not in the wind; then an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake; then a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire a still small voice.

That is the power of the Most High and of Christ: wind of extreme speed, an earthquake to catch up with it, then fire, and then he spoke in a still small voice. We do not know who we are dealing with; this is the same Most High who destroyed all but eight in the flood and rained fire on the cities of Sodom. Fear him who has the power to destroy the body.

When Elijah heard it he wrapped his face in his mantle and stood in the cave entrance, and the voice asked again, What doest thou here, Elijah? He answered the same, that he was zealous for the Lord and that he alone was left and they sought his life.

The Lord sent Elijah back to the wilderness of Damascus to anoint Hazael to be king over Syria, Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel, and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah to be prophet in his room. Him that escaped the sword of Hazael would Jehu slay, and him that escaped Jehu would Elisha slay.

The Most High was telling Elijah not to worry, for he had things set up: Syria would come against the northern kingdom, Jehu would rise up to slay Ahab and all his house, and Elisha would pick up where Elijah left off when it was his time to come home.

The Lord said he had left himself seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which had not bowed unto Baal. Elijah was not by himself; the Lord had people reserved who had not yet awakened, ordained to come in at a certain time for a certain purpose. It is the same today: our job is to preach the word, for we never know what video or flyer will wake up the ones the Lord has reserved.

Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle, like a cloak, upon him. Elisha left the oxen and ran after Elijah, asking to kiss his father and mother first, then he would follow.

Elisha returned, took a yoke of oxen and slew them, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave to the people, and they did eat; then he arose and followed Elijah and ministered unto him. He fed the people before he left and then he was gone on his mission, not turning back.
